sentences.text: Has a leap second ever been taken away? The IERS record says every one so far has been an addition, not a subtraction.

assertions.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

validation.text: Every leap second since UTC began in 1972 has been added to civil time; none has ever been taken away: the IERS table of TAI-UTC runs from 10 seconds on 1 January 1972 to 37 seconds on 1 January 2017, each value one second larger than the last, 27 steps in all.

supporting.note: The IERS table of TAI-UTC lists 28 values from 10 s on 1 January 1972 to 37 s on 1 January 2017, each exactly one second larger than the one before: every one of the 27 steps added a second and none subtracted one.
supporting.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

resolved.explanation: Figure decision-most-discussed-claims/sc01 draws only two stat tiles, 10 s/1972 and 37 s/2017 (the storyboard's own note calls these 'the endpoints, not the full run'), which are 27 seconds apart. The caption 'The IERS table's first and most recent values, each one second more than the last' is true of the 28-row table but, attached to a chart showing only those two endpoints, tells the reader the two displayed numbers are one second apart when they are 27 apart.
resolved.suggestion: Caption the two tiles for what they are, e.g. 'The IERS table's first and most recent values; every value between them is exactly one second more than the one before it,' rather than describing the two drawn values as one second apart.
